analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance to cover over-the-counter birth control pills without copays.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to three House committees, it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before Congress ended, despite 101 House Democratic sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health insurance plans to cover over-the-counter birth control pills without cost-sharing, even when a woman does not have a prescription, as soon as the FDA approves such a product for sale. It would also stop retailers from blocking or limiting a customer's access to daily oral birth control sold over the counter. Its premise is that easier access matters little if the pills are not affordable — so it pairs over-the-counter status with an insurance coverage guarantee.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who use birth control, especially those who struggle with its cost: the bill's findings cite a national survey finding that 1 in 3 women have struggled to afford birth control at some point, leading them to use it inconsistently [S3]. If the FDA approves an oral contraceptive for over-the-counter sale, insured women could pick it up without a prescription and without paying out of pocket [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and the Treasury to clarify that the Affordable Care Act's contraceptive coverage mandate includes over-the-counter FDA-approved contraceptives, even without a prescription, with no cost-sharing [S2] [S3].
Bars retailers that stock over-the-counter daily oral birth control from interfering with a customer's access to the product or to medically accurate information about it [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings note the ACA contraceptive benefit already extends no-cost coverage to about 62 million women, and this bill would extend that guarantee to an over-the-counter pill once one is approved [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor plans would absorb the cost of covering over-the-counter contraceptives without cost-sharing, potentially passing some of it into premiums. Retailers that stock such pills would take on new duties not to interfere with access. Uninsured women, who pay for birth control out of pocket, get no direct benefit from the coverage mandate.

drawbacks.text: The coverage requirement is a mandate on insurers and employer plans: someone pays for no-cost-sharing coverage, and the cost could flow into premiums for all enrollees [S2].

The bill does nothing by itself to make a pill available over the counter — it only requires coverage once the FDA approves such a product, so its practical effect depends entirely on future FDA action [S3].
It imposes new obligations on retailers, who can be required to grant access to the product and information about it, while the bill still lets them decline to sell if the customer cannot pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insured women, the benefits are concrete and immediate once an FDA-approved over-the-counter pill exists: no prescription visit, no out-of-pocket cost, and fewer access barriers. The costs are real but modest and diffuse — a small added coverage obligation for insurers and plan sponsors and light compliance duties for retailers. The bill's main design weakness is that it piggybacks on FDA approval that had not yet happened, so it guarantees nothing on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and Congress ended before it got any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on May 27, 2022, late in the 117th Congress, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means committees [S1] [S5].
100 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referrals [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off because the bill died: they never had to absorb the cost of covering over-the-counter contraceptives without cost-sharing. Women struggling to afford birth control gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 101 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; even so, the Democratic-controlled House never brought the bill out of committee.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They would have to cover FDA-approved over-the-counter contraceptives with no cost-sharing and no prescription, absorbing that cost in claims. That obligation is precisely what the bill would deliver to insured women, so the industry's cost in this bill is the public's benefit.

A coverage mandate would guarantee reimbursement for any over-the-counter pill they get approved, and the bill's sense-of-the-House section directly urges them to apply to the FDA for over-the-counter status. Their gain and the public's access gain point the same way.

Retailers stocking over-the-counter daily oral birth control could not interfere with a customer's access to the product or information about it, though they may still decline a sale to someone who cannot pay. A light but real constraint on how they manage the product.
